1: Good morning. Thank you, President and Professors, for the time you are giving me to present and discuss my thesis. My name is Mouad Louhichi. My thesis is titled Cooperative Game Theory for Explainable AI in Recommendation Systems: A Shapley Framework for Actionable Insight, supervised by Professor Mohamed Lazaar. It defends one idea: that Shapley-value attribution is not only a post-hoc explanation, but one formal method that can explain black-box clustering, stay consistent across levels and at scale, and finally act as an in-training signal inside a recommender.
2: I will walk you through five parts: introduction, context and problematic, the shared experimental protocol, then my three contributions, and finally the conclusion and perspectives. Each contribution follows the same structure: objectives, methodology, results, and findings. So you always know where we are.
3: Let us begin with the introduction. I will spend a few minutes on why explainability is not a nice-to-have but a core requirement for recommender systems, and I will define carefully what I mean by an actionable insight.
4: Three questions frame the whole work. First, these systems are everywhere: black-box systems shape what billions of people see, buy and watch every day, not only on streaming platforms but in e-commerce, news feeds and search. Second, the black box: even strong recommenders and clustering pipelines are hard to question. We see their outputs without knowing why a given item was chosen. Third, trust: transparency should be built into the model, not added after the fact. The core tension of the thesis is that as models gain power, they lose the transparency needed for trustworthy use. Throughout this work I treat accuracy and interpretability as two goals to meet together, not to trade against each other.
5: We frame the whole thesis around actionable insight. An explanation is actionable when it points to at least one factor that can be changed, when that change leads to a clear change in the model output, and when that factor is stated in the domain's own terms: a chemical variable for wine, a pollution indicator for air quality, a preference signal for recommendation. The key constraint is that it must not be a hidden latent code. This is what separates explanations that let a designer act from those that only describe what happened. By this definition, a good explanation is judged by whether it supports a real decision, not by whether it looks plausible.
6: The context is the move from simple to hypergraph recommenders. Matrix factorisation showed that latent factors could capture preferences, but those factors had no readable meaning. Graph and graph-neural-network models improved ranking by using connectivity, yet they replaced a hidden latent code with a hidden message-passing mechanism. Finally, hypergraph models added higher-order user-item-context relations, but they usually assume that every message counts the same. Each step added modelling power and removed transparency. This gap matters for trust, debugging and regulation: the EU AI Act, the OECD principles and the GDPR all ask for meaningful explanation. That is why a well-founded attribution method is needed, and why I will argue it should be part of the model itself rather than an add-on.
7: Recommendation is not a niche technique; it is infrastructure for everyday decisions. Streaming platforms decide what you watch next, music services what you hear, e-commerce what you buy, and social feeds what you read. Each system is very accurate, yet its reasoning is hidden from the user. Everywhere, and hidden: that is exactly what makes explainability a core requirement, and what motivates the three contributions that follow.
8: Now let us look more closely at the problem this thesis addresses. I will quickly go over the main approaches, then point out the main limitations and the five research questions, and finally map the three contributions to those questions.
9: A quick tour of the approaches we build on. Collaborative filtering works on the idea that similar users will like similar items, computed from the user side or the item side. Content-based filtering recommends items whose features match a profile, and hybrid methods combine both. Matrix factorisation splits the interaction matrix into latent factors: compact and effective, but hidden. Graph-based methods, including LightGCN and hypergraph extensions, pass information over an interaction structure and capture multi-hop or higher-order relations. Each one makes the model stronger, but each one makes interpretation harder in its own way: matrix factorisation hid the meaning of the latent dimensions; graph models left importance implicit; hypergraph models added higher-order relations but assumed all messages matter equally. That equal-messages assumption is one of the things I will challenge.
10: Four classical limitations. Data sparsity and scalability are the most cited: the user-item matrix is almost empty, so there is very little signal to learn from. Cold-start follows from that, because a new user or item has no history to learn from. Popularity bias and the resulting lack of diversity create a filter-bubble loop, where exposure leads to interaction, which leads to more exposure. And the most basic limitation, the one this thesis targets, is the lack of interpretability. For clustering the situation is even harder: methods give a local explanation or a global one but not both, they struggle to scale, and their explanations rarely stay consistent across levels of detail. That combination, no faithful local and global explanation, poor scaling, and no consistency across levels, is exactly the gap I work on.
11: Three main problems. First, lack of explainability: complex models are still hard to explain in a faithful and actionable way. Second, difficulty of scaling: local explanations do not carry over to multi-level structures or large datasets, so a method that works on a toy partition may break on hundreds of thousands of nested records. Third, weak link with learning: most explanations are post-hoc; they do not shape how the model learns, and they take no part in the accuracy-diversity-context trade-off the model is trying to satisfy. The thesis gap follows directly: the literature still lacks one cooperative-attribution framework that explains clustering faithfully, stays consistent across levels, and then works as an in-training signal in recommendation. My claim is that Shapley-value attribution can be that framework.
12: The overall aim is to develop, justify and evaluate a cooperative-game view of explainable AI for clustering and recommendation, using Shapley attribution both as an explanation method and as an in-training signal. Five research questions form the backbone. RQ1 asks how Shapley values can explain black-box clustering faithfully at instance and cluster level. RQ2 asks how that extends to large-scale, multi-level clustering while staying feasible and consistent. RQ3 asks whether cooperative attribution can move beyond post-hoc analysis and become part of how graph recommenders learn. RQ4 asks whether a recommender can improve ranking accuracy, context and diversity at the same time when importance comes from a cooperative-game utility. RQ5 is the thesis-level question: what do we gain when clustering explanation and recommendation learning are read as two stages of one shared view.
13: Three contributions, one thread. C1 sets up Shapley-based explanation for black-box clustering through a PCA, K-Means, LightGBM, TreeSHAP pipeline, and validates it on the wine quality dataset. C2 scales it to multi-level and large data, with cross-level SHAP aggregation, validated on the Beijing air-quality dataset. C3 is the strongest claim: DyHuCoG replaces post-hoc attribution with an in-training signal inside a hypergraph recommender, validated on MovieLens-1M and Amazon-Book. Each contribution answers its own research question, but they are designed to be read together as one argument that builds step by step. The thesis claim is that cooperative game theory works as one shared attribution view for explanation, optimisation and action, not that these are three unrelated papers.
14: Our thesis is a single claim: that Shapley-value attribution can work as one shared, explainable view across clustering and recommendation. The three contributions are not separate fixes but one argument that builds up: each applies the same cooperative-game logic at a different stage, from faithful clustering explanation to an in-training signal inside a recommender. That is what makes explanation part of the model itself, not a by-product attached after prediction.
15: Before the contributions, let me briefly cover the shared experimental setup. The purpose of this section is to show that my comparisons are fair: the datasets, the splitting and preprocessing, the baselines, the evaluation metrics, and the hardware.
16: Two clustering datasets and two recommendation datasets. For clustering I chose, on purpose, datasets with features that have a clear meaning, because the whole point of the method is to return attribution to the original variables. Wine Quality is a small, dense, chemically correlated dataset of almost five thousand samples with eleven features. Beijing Multi-Site Air Quality is a large, noisy dataset of over three hundred and eighty thousand hourly records, which varies with time and weather. For recommendation I used standard benchmark datasets with well-known baselines: MovieLens-1M, with roughly a million interactions and a density of 0.0447, and Amazon-Book, which is far sparser at 0.0006. The sparsity contrast is on purpose, because it stress-tests whether a Shapley-guided model helps most exactly when interaction data are weak.
17: Beyond scale, each dataset was chosen so that attribution lands in terms a domain expert can act on. Wine and Beijing give features with a clear meaning (chemistry, pollution); the two recommendation datasets give a density contrast that shows whether cooperative attribution helps most when interaction data are scarce. That is why the same explanatory logic can be validated across tabular clustering and recommendation without changing the mechanism.
18: Splitting is designed against leakage, because recommendation metrics are very sensitive to how you split. For clustering I use five-fold cross-validation to test the stability of the surrogate and the attribution. For recommendation I use a user-level, time-ordered holdout: interactions sorted by time per user, split seventy percent train, ten percent validation, twenty percent test. Evaluation uses leave-one-out, where the latest test positive per user is the target, ranked against sampled negatives. Because MovieLens-1M contains explicit ratings, I convert ratings greater than three into positive implicit feedback. Negatives are drawn from a popularity-aware distribution to produce harder negatives. Results are reported across five seeds, with early stopping on validation NDCG at twenty.
19: Baselines cover classical, neural, graph and hypergraph methods, exactly so that I can isolate the effect of cooperative attribution rather than a lucky model choice. For recommendation I compare against matrix factorisation, NCF, LightGCN, RecDCL, HCCF and HPCF, with HPCF as the strongest reference. For clustering interpretability I compare against a LIME-based surrogate pipeline. Ranking is measured with Precision at K, Recall at K, and NDCG at twenty as the main measure. On the diversity side I measure system-level catalogue coverage, and list-level intra-list diversity, defined as the average pairwise dissimilarity inside a ranked list. I want to stress that ILD is not there for show: it is built into the DyHuCoG coalition utility on purpose. Clustering quality is measured with Silhouette and Davies-Bouldin.
20: The hardware matters mainly because it explains some runtime figures I will quote later. All clustering, preprocessing and data loading run on an Intel Core i9-14900K with twenty-four cores. DyHuCoG training and inference run on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 with twenty-four gigabytes, with forty-eight gigabytes of RAM and a two-terabyte SSD. The software stack is Python 3.8, with scikit-learn for PCA and K-Means, LightGBM for the surrogate, SHAP for TreeSHAP, and PyTorch 2.0.1 for the recommendation model. I use Altair for interactive SHAP visualisation and report metrics at K equal to five, ten and twenty. Everything runs on standard academic hardware; nothing here needs industrial-scale compute.
21: Let us move to the first contribution: explaining black-box clustering with Shapley values. This contribution answers RQ1, and I will present it in four steps: objectives, methodology, results, findings.
22: Why start with clustering? Here the model creates its own structure, so the meaning of a cluster must be worked out after the fact. That makes clustering the hardest and most natural test bed for attribution. The gap is that explainable clustering is fragmented: methods favour a local or a global explanation, rarely both; they often fail to scale; and they rarely stay consistent across clusters. And since Shapley explanation is well established in supervised problems, its near absence from unsupervised clustering is striking. Our objectives are three: build a pipeline that gives a cluster-level explanation while keeping feature-level attribution; keep the meaning of the original feature space rather than a transformed latent space; and justify why Shapley is the right concept rather than an ad-hoc surrogate such as LIME.
23: RQ1 asks how Shapley values can explain black-box clustering faithfully at both instance and cluster level, and it breaks down into three objectives. O1 is a pipeline that produces a cluster-level explanation while keeping feature-level attribution, so the explanation is consistent rather than a single summary number. O2 requires that attribution stays in the original feature space: density, pH, acidity, sulfur dioxide, alcohol, because that is what makes it actionable for a domain expert. O3 is about justification: we must show why Shapley is the right allocation rule rather than an ad-hoc surrogate such as LIME. The next methodology slide shows how these three objectives are met.
24: We frame clustering as a cooperative game where the features are the players. The value function measures how well the data cluster when we use only the features in a given coalition: concretely, the value of coalition S is the Silhouette of K-Means run on the feature subset X_S, with a fixed k. I choose Silhouette because it is bounded, normalised and easy to interpret; Davies-Bouldin or Calinski-Harabasz would also be defensible. A feature then receives a high Shapley value when adding it improves separation, on average over all coalitions. The problem is that computing the Silhouette for every subset is combinatorial and not feasible even for a modest number of features, which is exactly why we need a bridge between the unsupervised partition and a practical attribution method.
25: The bridge is the heart of the method. TreeSHAP explains tree models; it cannot explain K-Means centroids. And explaining the PCA representation would move attribution away from the variables we care about. So we turn an unsupervised partition into a supervised task: once K-Means produces cluster labels, we train a LightGBM multiclass classifier to predict them from the original features, then apply TreeSHAP to that surrogate. This keeps attribution in the original feature space, which is what makes the explanation actionable. The key validity condition is surrogate fidelity: if the surrogate does not reproduce the partition well, the attribution is not faithful. We require a macro-F1 of around 0.82 as the floor.
26: The pipeline has five stages. Stage one is feature standardisation. Stage two is PCA, which I want to stress is used only as a computational and visual check; on purpose, it is not the explanatory space, because explaining principal components would defeat the purpose of actionable attribution. Stage three is K-Means-plus-plus with multi-criteria k selection, using the elbow method, Silhouette and Davies-Bouldin. Stage four is the LightGBM surrogate trained on the original features to predict the cluster labels. Stage five is TreeSHAP attribution in the original feature space, aggregated into global importance, cluster-specific profiles, and local force plots. The cost is dominated by PCA and repeated K-Means; TreeSHAP scales with tree count and depth rather than exponentially in the number of features, which is what makes the approach practical.
27: This is an honest and important point. We evaluate k from two to ten, and we select k equal to three on purpose, even though it is not the best geometry. With k equal to two we get a stronger Silhouette of 0.214 and a Davies-Bouldin of 1.775; with k equal to three the Silhouette drops to 0.144 and the Davies-Bouldin rises to 2.097. On raw geometry, two is the better partition. We choose three anyway, because three clusters support three distinct, chemically meaningful wine stories, far more actionable than a two-way split. I select the partition a domain expert would find useful, not the one that maximises a separation index. And to avoid a common confusion: the 0.63 Silhouette belongs to the Beijing dataset in Contribution II, not to this one.
28: The global SHAP ranking is led by density, followed by pH, fixed acidity, sulfur-dioxide-related variables and alcohol. These are exactly the variables a wine expert would point to as controlling structure, preservation and sensory balance. The important point is that this is not a random side effect of the classifier. Because the surrogate was trained to reproduce the partition from the original variables, and because TreeSHAP attributes in that original space, the recovered ranking matches a chemically meaningful structure. This is the strongest evidence that the pipeline is faithful: it recovers domain knowledge without being told to. It also shows the value of keeping attribution in the original feature space rather than in a reduced or latent space.
29: The cluster-specific profiles show that the solution is not only interpretable overall but also different from one cluster to the next. Each cluster has its own signature. Cluster zero is driven mainly by density and sulfur-dioxide-related variables; cluster one by acidity and pH effects; cluster two by a different balance of acidity, alcohol and related chemical attributes. The key point is that the same small set of variables comes back in all three clusters, but with different relative weights in each. This is the actionable insight: a cluster is not just a label, it is a distinct, domain-meaningful combination of drivers. It also shows the method supports both a global reading, which variable matters most overall, and a local, per-cluster reading, where the practical value lies.
30: This table sums up why we prefer Shapley over LIME. SHAP bases attribution on a cooperative-game allocation rule and satisfies four axioms: efficiency, so the whole explanation mass is allocated; symmetry, so equal contributors get equal credit; the null-player property, so a player with zero marginal effect gets zero; and additivity, so explanations add up across games. LIME fits a local surrogate and has no equivalent guarantee; it is sensitive to the perturbation design. SHAP supports both local and global explanation, whereas LIME is mainly local, and SHAP is much stronger for comparing clusters, which is central here. One caveat: in this surrogate pipeline, efficiency holds with respect to the LightGBM output, not directly to the Silhouette-based game. That is exactly why surrogate fidelity matters.
31: To answer RQ1 directly: yes. Shapley values explain a black-box partition faithfully, provided the surrogate has high fidelity, and consistently at cluster level. Each objective is met. O1 is met because the pipeline gives both a global reading, density, pH, acidity, sulfur dioxide, alcohol, and a per-cluster reading where the same drivers get different weights. O2 is met because attribution is returned to the original chemical variables, which is what makes it actionable. O3 is met because Shapley satisfies efficiency, symmetry, the null-player property and additivity, whereas LIME has no equivalent guarantee. The honest caveat is that efficiency holds with respect to the surrogate output, not directly to the Silhouette-based game, which is why surrogate fidelity is the critical validity condition.
32: C1 answers RQ1 with a yes. The key findings are four. Shapley values explain the black-box partition at both cluster level and instance level, tying each cluster's meaning to single feature contributions. They return attribution to the original chemical variables, density, pH, fixed acidity, sulfur dioxide, alcohol, rather than to a reduced or latent space, which is what makes the explanation actionable. Because the surrogate reproduces the partition from the original variables, the recovered ranking is chemically meaningful and faithful. And the approach has a solid theoretical basis: SHAP satisfies efficiency, symmetry, the null-player property and additivity, which LIME does not.
33: Let me be clear about the scope. First, the explanation depends on the fidelity of the LightGBM surrogate; it is not a direct mechanism of the K-Means geometry. Second, the approach is limited to tabular data. Third, and most important for what follows, it is single-level: it cannot yet handle consistency across levels, meaning it cannot explain how feature importance changes between a partition and its sub-partitions. And the surrogate plus representative-instance reporting smooths out some variation between single observations. These limits are the starting point for Contribution II.
34: The takeaway is that Shapley attribution works as one well-founded lens for explaining an unsupervised partition, and that keeping attribution in the original feature space is what makes it actionable. But real data are rarely single-level: broad groups contain nested sub-groups, and a variable can be globally important yet locally uninformative. That flat limitation directly motivates Contribution II: can the explanation logic be scaled to multi-level, large-scale clustering without losing consistency?
35: This brings us to the second contribution: scaling the explanation logic to multi-level, large-scale clustering. It answers RQ2, and the central concern is not only scale but several levels of detail.
36: C2 asks whether the C1 logic survives scale and hierarchy. Large real-world data contain structure at more than one level of detail: broad groups at the top, nested sub-groups inside them. A variable can be globally important yet locally uninformative, or the reverse, so a flat explanation is true but incomplete: it cannot show how importance changes as you zoom in. The chapter adds three things. First, a truly multi-level workflow, not a rerun of the single-level pipeline. Second, a formal cross-level consistency argument, Proposition 6.1, so that differences across levels can be interpreted rather than ruled out as inconsistency. Third, validation on a very different large-scale dataset, Beijing air quality, to test whether the method generalises beyond the small, correlated wine dataset.
37: RQ2 asks whether the C1 logic survives scale and hierarchy while staying feasible and consistent, and it breaks down into three objectives. O1 is a truly multi-level workflow: coarse clustering at the top and nested sub-groups inside, so that attribution stays readable inside a cluster, across sub-clusters, and across the levels. O2 is a formal cross-level consistency argument, Proposition 6.1, so that differences across levels can be interpreted rather than ruled out as inconsistency. O3 is an empirical check on generality: validation on a very different large-scale dataset, Beijing air quality, rather than the small, chemically correlated wine dataset.
38: The multi-level architecture works recursively: we learn a coarse clustering on the full dataset, then split each cluster again where it makes sense, which gives a nested structure. For each level we train a level-specific surrogate and compute SHAP values in the same original feature space. The cross-level aggregation is, on purpose, not a naive average: it respects cluster size and nesting structure. A parent-level attribution is an expectation over the explanations of its children, so a coarse-level importance reflects the size-weighted contributions of the clusters it contains. One methodological point: the hierarchy here is a practical analysis tool. I am not claiming the data have a true, natural hierarchy of levels; the nested structure is a computational and interpretive tool, and Proposition 6.1 is stated with that in mind.
39: Proposition 6.1 is the mathematical heart of the contribution. Let Phi at level l, in cluster c, for feature j, be the expected absolute SHAP importance over the examples in that cluster, and let w sub c-prime be the relative size of a child cluster within its parent. For a strict nested hierarchy on a consistent feature space, the parent's expected absolute importance equals the sum over its children of the child's relative size times the child's expected absolute importance, plus a residual epsilon that comes from surrogate mismatch and vanishes under perfect fidelity. The derivation uses the law of total expectation and the fact that the children partition the parent. The key point: it does not claim explanations are identical across levels; it says differences can be interpreted rather than ruled out as inconsistency. That makes a multi-level explanation self-consistent and auditable.
40: On Beijing, the k-selection criteria agree much more strongly than on wine, and this is worth stressing. The full dataset clusters cleanly into k equal to three, with a Silhouette of about 0.63 and a Davies-Bouldin of about 0.55. Recall that this is where the 0.63 figure comes from: it belongs to Beijing, not to the wine partition, whose Silhouette is 0.144. The low Davies-Bouldin means the clusters rarely overlap. The PCA projection, using two components, is used only for visual inspection. I also tested sensitivity: the conclusions are robust to small changes in k, in the number of projection dimensions, and in the surrogate depth; only low-ranked variables shift. So the finding is not a side effect of one parameter choice.
41: The global ranking is rich. The dominant features are temperature, dew point and pressure, followed by carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, PM10 and PM2.5. It is striking that it is not only the pollutant concentrations that dominate. Weather variables play a central role in the structure, because temperature, dew point and pressure control dispersion, trapping and sunlight-driven chemistry. In other words, they set the atmospheric conditions under which pollution builds up. This is exactly the kind of insight that flat summaries often miss: a naive ranking of pollutant concentrations would overlook the fact that the weather is what sets the regime. It is a good example of why attribution in the original variable space is valuable.
42: The force plots reveal three representative regimes, and this is where the interpretation becomes concrete. Regime A is a warm, sunlight-driven regime, where ozone, temperature and dew point stand out; this is typical of summer photochemical smog. Regime B is a wintertime smog regime, dominated by carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide and particulate matter, with low wind speed limiting dispersion. Regime C is a comparatively clean-air regime, linked to favourable weather and weak pollutant signals. The value is not only in showing that these regimes exist; it is in showing which combinations of variables define each one. That is the actionable insight: an air-quality analyst can see the specific drivers of a given pollution episode and act on them.
43: This is the main payoff of the chapter, and the reason a flat explanation is not enough. At the coarse level, temperature and dew point dominate, because they separate the broad atmospheric regimes. Inside single clusters, the informative variables shift to carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, PM10, wind speed, pressure or ozone. This change is not a contradiction. It is exactly what a multi-level explanation should reveal. The parent-level story is regime selection; the cluster-level story is variation within a regime. A variable can be globally important yet locally uninformative inside a sub-cluster. Proposition 6.1 lets us read these shifts as meaningful structure rather than noise; a flat, single-level explanation would present them as a conflict, whereas our framework makes them consistent.
44: The same logic works on both a small, dense, chemically correlated dataset and a large, noisy, environmental one, which supports the generality of the approach. It is not tied to one special property of wine chemistry. I also compared against the SHAP-based clustering literature: our Beijing partition reaches a Silhouette of about 0.63, whereas Gramegna and Giudici, working on credit-risk data, report around 0.37. Against LIME, we see weaker consistency across levels and less stable local stories for multi-level reasoning. I want to be careful here: these are comparative observations rather than a full benchmark, but they support the claim that a cooperative-attribution approach produces more structured, more consistent explanations for multi-level clustering.
45: To answer RQ2 directly: yes, within bounds. Shapley-based clustering explanation can scale to multi-level, large-scale settings without losing consistency, provided the hierarchy is modelled explicitly and the approximation is transparent. O1 is met: we obtain a multi-level explanation that does not collapse into a single flat summary. O2 is met: Proposition 6.1 gives a formal cross-level consistency argument, so the regime-level and cluster-level stories do not conflict. O3 is met: the approach validates on Beijing air quality, a large, noisy dataset that varies over time, which supports generality. The honest bound is that the model is still an explanation of a pre-computed partition; it does not yet influence learning itself. That is the bridge to Contribution III.
46: C2 answers RQ2 with a yes. The key findings are four. The explanation scales to a multi-level structure without collapsing into a single flat summary, because the hierarchy is modelled explicitly rather than flattened. Proposition 6.1 provides a formal cross-level consistency argument, so that differences across levels can be read as meaningful structure rather than ruled out as noise. The approach generalises to a very different large-scale dataset, Beijing air quality, which is far noisier and changes far more over time than the small correlated wine data. And the method produces parent-level regime-selection stories together with cluster-level, within-regime variation.
47: The limitations are just as clear. The clustering stays static even though the Beijing data are temporal, so the dynamics are not used. The surrogate-based SHAP plus representative-instance reporting smooths out variation between single observations, so some richness is lost. The whole approach is limited to tabular data. And, most important for what follows, the model is still an explanation of a pre-computed partition: it does not yet influence learning itself. This is the bridge to Contribution III.
48: The takeaway is that Shapley attribution stays consistent across levels of detail, provided the hierarchy is made explicit. Explanations become interpretable at scale, not only for a single flat partition, which is exactly where the literature was weakest. But the attribution is still post-hoc: it explains a partition that was already computed, and it never influences how the model learns. That is the limit that motivates Contribution III: can cooperative attribution move beyond explanation and become part of how a recommender learns?
49: The third and main contribution introduces DyHuCoG, a Dynamic Hypergraph Cooperative Game, where Shapley attribution becomes an in-training signal inside a hypergraph recommender rather than a post-hoc explanation. It answers RQ3 and RQ4.
50: C3 is the flagship contribution and the conceptual shift of the whole thesis. The gap is that graph and hypergraph recommenders treat message importance as either uniform or attention-weighted, with no well-founded account of marginal contribution. Diversity is usually a secondary goal or a re-ranking heuristic, not part of the core learning problem; and interpretability is added after prediction rather than built into the objective. Our objectives are three: formulate recommendation as a cooperative game in which users, items and contexts are players; embed preference-aware Monte Carlo Shapley estimates into hypergraph message passing so that attribution directly shapes how information flows; and improve ranking accuracy, coverage and intra-list diversity together. The strongest claim is not that we explain a recommender; it is that attribution becomes an in-training signal.
51: C3 answers RQ3 and RQ4 together, and it is the conceptual shift of the thesis. RQ3 asks whether cooperative attribution can move beyond post-hoc explanation and become part of how a graph recommender learns. RQ4 asks whether a recommender can improve ranking accuracy, context and diversity at the same time when importance is estimated by a cooperative-game utility. Both map to three objectives. O1 is to formulate recommendation as a cooperative game in which users, items and contexts are players. O2 is to embed preference-aware Monte Carlo Shapley estimates into hypergraph message passing, so attribution directly shapes how information flows. O3 is to improve ranking, coverage and intra-list diversity together, not one at the expense of another.
52: We model recommendation as a cooperative game whose players are users, items and contexts. The hypergraph has vertices drawn from this same set, and hyperedges encode user-item-context interactions, with dynamic edge weights derived from Shapley estimates. A coalition is the set of entities taking part in a recommendation episode, and the coalition value measures the quality of the recommendation that this coalition can achieve. The task is top-N recommendation: we produce a ranked list for a user that balances relevance, diversity and contextual fit. This mirrors the clustering formulation, but with a value function built for recommendation. That parallel is intended, and it is one of the thesis-level contributions: the same cooperative-game logic applies to both tasks.
53: The coalition utility combines ranking quality, diversity and context: a weighted sum of NDCG at twenty, a diversity term and a context score, with weights summing to one. The key point is that this is the same trade-off the recommender must satisfy and also the trade-off from which attribution is computed, so the explanatory game and the predictive objective are aligned by design. We add a preference-consistency bonus proportional to the sum of user-item similarities in the coalition. Alpha, beta and gamma were grid-searched to 0.60, 0.25 and 0.15, with the preference coefficient at 0.20, and NDCG varies by under one and a half percent around that point. One honest boundary: coalition evaluation is limited to the interaction episode, a few dozen players, not the full catalogue.
54: Exact Shapley computation is combinatorial and not feasible for a real recommender, so we use a Monte Carlo estimator that averages, over M sampled coalitions, the difference between the value with a player and the value without it; the preference-aware variant applies the same estimator to the preference-weighted utility. It is unbiased, with variance decaying as sigma squared over M, so the mean squared error goes as one over M and the absolute error as one over root M. We chose M equal to fifty: mean squared error about one point four times ten to the minus five, and roughly ninety-nine percent accuracy. Because preferences change, the estimates are refreshed every ten batches, about forty-nine updates per epoch, and smoothed with an exponential moving average, so attribution adapts without making training too sensitive to a single estimate.
55: The architecture is the decisive move. The base propagation is standard hypergraph message passing; the Shapley-weighted version weights each message by a normalised Shapley coefficient, dividing by the sum of coefficients over the neighbourhood. I clip and exponentially smooth the estimates before normalising, which keeps the sparse setting stable. Layer fusion combines embeddings across layers with learned coefficients. On top of that, an interaction-level attention gate blends the Shapley-weighted score with the standard inner-product score, acting as a stabiliser; a context-aware score then adds a context term. The essential point is that the model is told not only who is connected to whom, but how much each coalition is worth, and that worth directly controls how information flows. That is what sets it apart from a post-hoc explainer.
56: The composite loss combines four terms. The recommendation loss is Bayesian Personalised Ranking, a pairwise objective suited to implicit feedback. The diversity loss is an intra-list diversity regulariser that penalises redundant ranked lists. The context loss aligns the context embedding with the context-node representation. And the regularisation term is weight decay. Negatives are drawn from a popularity-aware distribution, with periodic hard-negative refresh, and optimisation uses Adam. The main point I want to make is alignment: the model is trained to optimise the same accuracy-diversity-context balance that later determines cooperative attribution. So the explanation is not a separate check; it is a direct read-out of the objective the model is already optimising. This is what makes the explanation faithful by design.
57: This is the headline result, and I would ask you to read it carefully because it shows ranking and diversity improving together. On MovieLens-1M, the strongest baseline HPCF reaches an NDCG at twenty of 0.2528 and a recall of 0.2098; DyHuCoG improves these to 0.2775 and 0.2362, plus nine point seven seven percent in NDCG and plus twelve point five eight percent in recall. At the same time, coverage rises from 0.342 to 0.397 and intra-list diversity from 0.461 to 0.516. On Amazon-Book, which is much sparser, the relative gains are larger: plus thirteen point three three percent NDCG and plus sixteen point one six percent recall, with coverage up by nearly thirty percent. The sparser the data, the larger the gain: exactly the pattern you would expect if Shapley-driven weighting is most valuable when the signal is weak.
58: This slide sums up the relative gains over the strongest baseline, and the key message is that DyHuCoG improves ranking accuracy, coverage and diversity at the same time: it does not give up one for the others. The largest relative gains appear on the sparser Amazon-Book dataset, in line with the hypothesis that Shapley-guided weighting helps most exactly when interaction data are weak. Together these results are evidence that the accuracy-diversity trade-off, often treated as fixed by nature, can in fact be moved if attribution is handled as a first-class part of the learning objective. NDCG up, recall up, coverage up, diversity up: that combination is the core empirical claim of the third contribution.
59: Both levels of diversity improve. On MovieLens-1M, catalogue coverage rises from 0.342 to 0.397, a sixteen percent improvement, and intra-list diversity from 0.461 to 0.516, an eleven point nine percent improvement. On Amazon-Book, coverage rises from 0.259 to 0.336, nearly thirty percent, and intra-list diversity from 0.535 to 0.602. In practice this means a smaller filter-bubble effect and more discovery for the user. The point I want to stress: both diversity metrics improve while NDCG and recall also improve, so we are not trading accuracy for diversity. The model shows more of the catalogue, recommends less redundant lists, and ranks better at the same time. That is the strongest evidence that diversity is a real objective here, not a post-hoc re-ranking heuristic.
60: This ablation isolates each component, and every component contributes. The full model reaches 0.2775 NDCG at twenty on MovieLens-1M. Removing the Shapley value drops it to 0.2647, a four point six percent loss. Removing the hypergraph structure drops it to 0.2586, a six point eight percent loss. Removing the attention gate costs three point five percent. Removing context causes the largest single loss at eight point two percent, in line with context providing the basis on which Shapley weighting operates. Removing diversity costs five point eight percent. The same pattern holds on Amazon-Book, with context removal again the largest. The four to six percent drop when Shapley is removed supports the argument that marginal-contribution estimation is essential, not there for show.
61: The attribution cost is reasonable, and I report it openly because it matters for real use. On MovieLens-1M, DyHuCoG takes about two thousand seconds to train versus roughly eleven hundred for HPCF, about one point seven eight times. Inference is one point eight four milliseconds per query on MovieLens and eight point five two on Amazon, well within real-time requirements. Memory is slightly higher, four point four gigabytes versus four point one. The per-epoch cost scales with the number of layers, the embedding dimension and the Monte Carlo budget. On Shapley convergence, M equal to fifty gives ninety-nine percent accuracy, while M equal to one hundred gives ninety-nine point five with diminishing returns. So fifty is the right operating point, balancing accuracy against cost.
62: I also checked that the improvements are statistically significant and large enough to matter. I ran paired t-tests on per-user NDCG at twenty across six thousand and forty users, comparing DyHuCoG against every baseline, with Holm-Bonferroni correction. Against HPCF, the t-statistic is 46.38, Cohen's d is 1.33, and the p-value is on the order of ten to the minus two hundred and seventy. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is also significant at p less than 0.001. The effect sizes are large, and that matters: with six thousand users, even a tiny difference can look significant, so reporting the effect size shows the improvement is not only a large-sample effect. I should be careful about scope: these tabulated paired tests apply only to MovieLens-1M; the Amazon-Book results remain descriptive.
63: DyHuCoG also improves the settings where recommenders are at their weakest: cold-start. For users with five or fewer interactions, NDCG at twenty is about 0.061, roughly ten percent over HPCF; for cold-start items about 0.057, a gain of roughly nine point six percent. Across datasets the improvement holds at plus nine point nine percent on MovieLens, plus fourteen point eight on Amazon, and plus eleven point eight on Yelp2018, which I use only as an extra robustness check. On interpretability, the model produces a SHAP waterfall that breaks a recommendation down into the same ranking, diversity, context and preference components used during training, so the explanation is faithful by design rather than an outside approximation. And Shapley measures marginal utility rather than raw frequency, so weak but informative interactions keep their influence, which reduces popularity bias.
64: To answer RQ3 and RQ4 directly: yes. RQ3 gets a yes because attribution is no longer a post-hoc check but an in-training signal that directly shapes message passing. RQ4 gets a yes because ranking, coverage and diversity improve together rather than trading against each other. Each objective is met. O1: recommendation is formulated as a cooperative game with users, items and contexts as players. O2: preference-aware Monte Carlo Shapley is embedded into hypergraph message passing. O3: we gain about nine point nine percent on MovieLens and fourteen point eight percent on Amazon, with higher coverage and diversity. The strongest claim is that the explanation is faithful by design, because it reads out the same components the model already optimises. Within the stated limits, compute overhead, dependence on context, and the early-2026 baseline set, the claim stands.
65: C3 answers RQ3 and RQ4, and makes the strongest claim of the thesis. Cooperative attribution can move beyond post-hoc analysis and become part of how a recommender learns, letting it balance accuracy, diversity and context more effectively. The key findings are that ranking, coverage and diversity improve together, NDCG, recall, coverage and intra-list diversity all rise on both datasets, so the accuracy-diversity trade-off is not fixed by nature. The largest gains appear on the sparsest data, Amazon-Book, exactly the setting where Shapley-driven weighting is most valuable, and the improvement is statistically large against the strongest baseline.
66: The limitations must be stated honestly. There is a measurable compute overhead, roughly one point seven eight times the training time of the strongest baseline, HPCF. The method depends on having meaningful context available. The Monte Carlo Shapley estimator could be improved by variance reduction. The ablation removes one component at a time, so it does not test combinations. And the baselines were fixed in early 2026, so I claim superiority only against the tested baselines. Within those bounds, the claim stands.
67: The takeaway is the conceptual shift of the thesis. Attribution is a first-class part of the learning objective, not a post-hoc check, and the explanation is a direct read-out of the objective the model already optimises. That is what makes it faithful by design rather than an outside approximation. And because Shapley values rest on four clear axioms, this view fits well with the transparency and accountability requirements of new AI regulation. This is the central claim worth defending: explanation should be part of the model itself.
68: Let me now bring everything together. I will present a synthesis of the three contributions, the published papers, the honest limitations, the future directions, and finally a clear statement of the thesis answer.
69: Three contributions, one thread. The synthesis table shows how each contribution builds on the previous one. C1 makes hidden structure easy to understand: it introduces a Shapley-based pipeline that explains black-box clustering faithfully, with faithful, chemistry-consistent cluster attribution on wine. C2 keeps that explanation consistent at scale and across levels: it introduces cross-level SHAP aggregation and Proposition 6.1, and shows that differences between levels can be interpreted rather than ruled out as inconsistency. C3 carries the same attribution logic inside the learning of a recommender, using preference-aware Shapley as an in-training signal, so that accuracy, coverage and diversity improve together. The common thread is that cooperative attribution is a single mechanism used for explanation, for interpretation and for optimisation, not three unrelated tools.
70: The thesis brings together three peer-reviewed publications, and it is worth mapping them to the chapters. Paper I, on Shapley values for explaining the black-box nature of machine-learning model clustering, is published in Procedia Computer Science in 2023 and corresponds to Chapter five. Paper II, on game theory meeting explainable AI for understanding black-box models, is published in IJACSA in 2025 and corresponds to Chapter six. Paper III, DyHuCoG, is published in IJIES in 2026 and corresponds to Chapter seven. What the thesis adds on top of the three papers is the multi-level formalisation, the cross-chapter comparisons, and the explicit mapping to the five research questions. In other words, the thesis is one argument that builds up, not only a bound collection of three papers.
71: Let me state the limitations honestly. On computation, exact Shapley is not feasible, so every contribution relies on approximation, surrogates, or limited reporting. On method, the clustering chapters depend on surrogate fidelity, and the recommendation results depend on stable approximate contributions and meaningful context. On experiments, the clustering work is limited to tabular data and the recommendation work is offline: no multimodal, sequential or online setting, and no dedicated user study of actionability. And on the claim itself, I want to be exact. I am not claiming one fully unified framework that removes all tension between accuracy and interpretability; I am claiming a shared view, a common attribution language, that is consistent and productive across the three tasks. That is the honest boundary of the thesis.
72: Future work turns the limitations into a concrete agenda. First, scalable cooperative attribution: lower-variance Shapley estimators, learned proposal distributions, and adaptive refresh rules, to close the compute gap. Second, online and streaming recommendation: truly incremental settings with graphs that keep changing and delayed feedback, which would also address the static-graph limitation. Third, richer user-centred evaluation: I would like to test whether these explanations measurably improve analyst judgement, user trust, quality of action, or perceived fairness, which is the natural test of the actionable part of my definition. Fourth, broader trustworthy-AI and fairness evaluation: exposure fairness, transparency requirements, and auditing for governance, which connects the work to the EU AI Act, the OECD principles and the GDPR.
73: To close: the thesis answer is that cooperative game theory can serve as a shared methodological view for actionable explanation across clustering and recommendation. The key outcomes are four. Shapley attribution provides a common formal language for assigning importance to features, interactions and contexts. It gives faithful clustering explanation, consistent multi-level explanation, and contribution-aware recommendation learning. And most important, it moves explanation from a comment added later to a method: from post-hoc description to in-training guidance. Because Shapley values rest on four clear axioms, this view fits well with the transparency and accountability requirements of new AI regulation. I believe this is the central claim worth defending: that explanation should be part of the model itself, not a by-product attached after prediction.
